title: Redwood structured output & function calling demo
summary: Redwood AE/SE demo of structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool calling for NovaBank. Showed Console examples, API usage, guardrails/schema enforcement, and tool integration patterns. Customer asked about deterministic JSON, validation, security (KMS/SSO/SOC2), and latency vs cost tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: send security package, sandbox key, sample schema cookbook, and schedule a 2-week POC/benchmark run.
topics: latency vs cost and Dedicated vs Hosted
action_items: Alex Nguyen: Share pricing summary and breakout for hosted vs dedicated (due 2026-11-20)
Priya Shah: Send sample JSON schema cookbook + Console export link (due 2026-11-19)
Redwood SE Team: Provision sandbox API key and small Dedicated bench cluster access (due 2026-11-23)
Hannah Kim (NovaBank): Provide list of compliance contacts and SCIM/SSO metadata (due 2026-11-22)

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-18 15:00 PST, Duration ~52 minutes. Attendees: Alex Nguyen (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam Carter (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (NovaBank CTO), Maya Lopez (NovaBank ML Eng), Hannah Kim (NovaBank Sec Ops), Evan Brooks (Prod).

Summary: quick demo of Redwood structured output JSON mode, function/tool calling, and Console guardrails. Showed a sample e-commerce to bank integration pattern, a ticketing tool call, and a vault/KMS note. Customer asked about deterministic JSON, failure modes, and security. Lots of cross talk and a few mis-transcriptions.

00:00 Alex Nguyen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account. Quick roll call, then Priya will jump into the structured output demo. Hi Daniel, Maya, Hannah, Evan, can you hear us okay?
00:09 Daniel Park: Yeah loud and clear, thanks Alex. Thanks for fitting us in, we carved out time to see how structured outputs and tool calling could help with our fraud ops and customer support flows.
00:18 Alex Nguyen: Awesome. Priya, over to you.
00:20 Priya Shah: Great thanks Alex. Hi team, I'm Priya, I'll run through JSON mode, schema enforcement, and function calling. We'll show the Console and API patterns, and then Liam will share a quick bench sketch. I'll start with a simple schema example so you can see how we guarantee structured responses.
00:38 Priya Shah: So here's a toy schema for a support-ticket creation call — fields: ticket_id string, priority enum low|medium|high, customer_id string, summary string, tags array. We're using Redwood's structured_output param which pins a schema and a strict mode that, um, enforces output to match. When strict is on the model will either return the JSON or an explicit error if it can't comply.
00:58 Maya Lopez: Quick question — what's the determinism here? If model hallucinate or gets partial, how do you ensure the JSON is consistent each time? We run automated parsers so this is critical.
01:10 Priya Shah: Great point. There are a couple levers: temperature control, logit bias, and deterministic decoding options; plus Redwood's validator layer post-generation. We can run validation hooks and optionally call a low-cost deterministic reranker or constrained decoding path. In practice we recommend temp <= 0.2 for strict schemas, and enable the validator which will either coerce or fail with structured error for deterministic handling.
01:36 Hannah Kim: And if it fails you have a standard error payload so our pipeline can decide retry vs fallback?
01:42 Priya Shah: Exactly, we returned a structured error object with error_code and diagnostics, and there's a pre-built retry policy in the Console; you can set it to fallback to a simpler template or call a tooling function instead.
01:53 Alex Nguyen: Also worth noting, for high-stability use cases we demo dedicated instances or pinned model variants — the results are more consistent and latency is predictable.
02:02 Evan Brooks: When you say dedicated, is that Redwood Dedicated or self-hosted? Latency targets and cost are both big for us.
02:09 Alex Nguyen: Redwood Dedicated — reserved GPU pools with predictable throughput. We'll share pricing but general rule: Dedicated lowers p99 and variance but has a higher fixed cost; hosted is lower upfront. We'll send a cost/latency tradeoff sheet after.
02:23 Liam Carter: Ok switching windows — here's the Console. On the left is the model route config, you can toggle structured_output "schema" and choose strict vs permissive. I'm going to paste a live example: create_ticket schema and then call the API directly from Console.
02:38 [keyboard sounds] Liam Carter: Sending sample request... and here's the response — clean JSON: {"ticket_id":"TCK-20261118-009","priority":"high","customer_id":"CUST-103","summary":"card declined while retrying auth","tags": ["payments","auth"]}. You can also see the validation trace below showing exact token positions that matched the schema.
03:02 Maya Lopez: Hmm the token trace is helpful — does that mean we could map output errors back to specific prompt tokens for debugging?
03:10 Priya Shah: Yep, exactly. The tracing hooks give token-level alignment so you can surface which part of the prompt caused deviation. That helps when fine-tuning prompt templates or building prompt engineering guardrails.
03:22 Daniel Park: Can you show tool/function calling — like if we want the model to call our ticket API or a search tool for KB articles?
03:29 Priya Shah: Sure. Two patterns: function-calling (model returns structured function args which Redwood then executes), and tool-calling where the model can request external tools and Redwood orchestrates the call with RBAC and secrets injection. I'll demo a function 'create_ticket' — schema for args is validated, then Redwood runtime executes a webhook to your endpoint.
03:49 Priya Shah: Example: model returns {"function":"create_ticket","args":{"customer_id":"CUST-103","summary":"...","priority":"high"}} then Redwood will POST to your secured webhook URL with an HMAC header. You get an execution record and audit log.
04:05 Hannah Kim: Security — what's in that audit log? Is the payload redactable? And how do we handle PII and KMS?
04:13 Priya Shah: Good questions. Audit logs include failed/successful calls, timestamps, model version, route, and a hash of the payload. For PII you can configure automatic redaction rules in the Console or use tokenization hooks. For encryption, Redwood integrates with customer KMS/HSM for key wrap; data at rest can be encrypted with your keys. We'll include the security pack with details.
04:35 Daniel Park: Great. One more on tool calling — can the model chain multiple tools? e.g., lookup account -> create ticket -> send notification?
04:44 Priya Shah: Yes, Redwood supports multi-step tool chains and orchestrated function calls. We provide a stateful call context so you can maintain session-level KV for the sequence and trace each tool invocation. The Console shows the call graph and latency breakdown per tool.
04:58 Evan Brooks: So how are secrets injected securely? We're not comfortable with plaintext webhooks.
05:05 Priya Shah: Secrets are injected at runtime by the Redwood agent. Your webhook receives a signed payload; Redwood never stores plaintext secrets in logs, and you can configure per-route secret scopes and rotate keys via KMS.
05:18 Maya Lopez: Can we enforce schema at the tool boundary as well? e.g., if model asks to call 'update_account' ensure args are within allowed fields?
05:25 Priya Shah: Yes — each tool has a declared input schema and Redwood validators will block calls that don't match. We also have RBAC so only certain model routes can call sensitive tools.
05:36 Liam Carter: Quick bench note — tool calls add latency (external network), we measure per-call and you can set a timeout policy. For internal tools on the same VPC it's very low, for external HTTP it's variable.
05:49 Daniel Park: About latency — with JSON strict mode and low temp, do you see higher p99 than freeform text?
05:55 Priya Shah: Slightly, sometimes decoding constraints add a bit of tail. That's where batching and Dedicated pins help. Also you can use a structured-output specialized kernel (we have optimized paths) to reduce overhead.
06:08 Maya Lopez: Could you show an example where the model does a search+tool chain then formats a final JSON response for our downstream pipelines?
06:15 Priya Shah: Yep. I'll run a live demo: prompt asks model to search KB for 'chargeback policy' and then create a summarized JSON answer with citations and a recommended next_action field — then call notify_ticketing if required.
06:28 [typing] Priya Shah: Sending request... model returns a function call to 'kb_search' with args, we execute, get results, then model calls 'create_ticket' with the assembled args. Final structured output arrives: {"summary":"Policy says...","citations": [{"doc_id":"kb-78","snippet":"..."}],"recommended_action":"escalate"}.
06:52 Daniel Park: Nice. The citations field is super helpful. How do you prevent hallucinated citations?
06:58 Priya Shah: We tie citations to the retriever — we return doc ids and snippets from your retriever. The model is forced to reference the retrieval results; plus the validator checks that citation ids exist in the returned search block.
07:12 Hannah Kim: From compliance angle, can we keep all tooling within our VPC or on-prem? We have restrictions on sending logs to third party regions.
07:20 Alex Nguyen: Yes, Redwood Private supports VPC/on-prem deployments with customer-managed networking. We'll also provide an on-prem package for air-gapped needs. For POCs we usually run in a customer-specific VPC with private endpoints.
07:33 Maya Lopez: Awesome. Next — developer ergonomics: does Redwood provide SDKs for function calling and schema management?
07:39 Liam Carter: Yep, SDKs for Python/Node/Go. We have utilities to register schemas, preview validation in Console, and an infra-as-code plugin to sync route configs. We'll share snippets.
07:50 Evan Brooks: What about model versioning and rollouts? If we lock a schema, how do rollouts handle variant models?
07:56 Priya Shah: We do model pinning per-route. Rollouts are canary/A-B with automatic rollback on regression. If a new model breaks a schema, the validator will flag and can block the rollout automatically depending on policy.
08:09 Daniel Park: Real quick, for our internal pipelines we need guaranteed JSON fields — if the model can't produce them, we'd prefer it return an explicit error rather than malformed JSON.
08:18 Priya Shah: That's the strict mode behavior — explicit structured error with diagnostics. You can also set coercion rules to fill defaults, or drop to a deterministic fallback that calls your own enrichment service.
08:31 Maya Lopez: Could you show logging and cost visibility for a route that uses function calling and structured output?
08:35 Liam Carter: On the Console -> Routes page you get token-level cost estimates, per-call tool execution cost, and third-party call egress. Here's an example route: 230ms median, 1.1s p99 including an external webhook, and cost breakdown by tokens+tool egress.
08:52 Daniel Park: we'll need that to build a cost model for our fraud ops flows. We'll share sample traffic patterns.
08:58 Evan Brooks: On security again — do you support SCIM/SSO and fine-grained RBAC?
09:03 Alex Nguyen: Yes SSO (SAML/OIDC) and SCIM provisioning, plus RBAC at route and tool level. We map roles to routes and only allow admin audit reads if configured. We'll include a sample RBAC policy in the security pack.
09:15 Maya Lopez: Can you run a quick failure scenario where the model hallucinated and created a ticket with incorrect customer_id, show how Redwood's validator & audit log help debug?
09:24 Priya Shah: Sure — I'll simulate a bad response. Here, model returned customer_id CUST-999 but retriever returned CUST-103. Validator flagged mismatch and returned error_code:SCHEMA_MISMATCH with diagnostics: expected customer_id from retrieval. In the audit log you can see the failed attempt and the raw tokens; we also attach the retriever hits.
09:46 Daniel Park: Good. That will make our ops teams happy. A couple of procurement questions: contract terms, data retention, and can you sign our DPA?
09:56 Alex Nguyen: We have standard DPA and we sign enterprise DPAs; retention is configurable per-route. We'll loop legal and share the template.
10:06 Evan Brooks: For a POC, what's the minimal timeline and resources needed? We want to run a small bench with ~1000 requests/day to simulate our peak.
10:14 Liam Carter: For that volume hosted easily supports it. If you're testing deterministic JSON and p99, we can provision a small Dedicated bench cluster for more stable tail metrics. Typically 1-2 weeks to get data and validate.
10:25 Maya Lopez: Can you provide a sample schema cookbook? We have complex nested objects for settlements and chargebacks.
10:31 Priya Shah: Yes, Priya will send the cookbook and a few real-world schema patterns for finance use-cases.
10:37 Alex Nguyen: Ok quick recap and next steps — Daniel, Hannah, Evan, we're going to send security docs, sandbox key, pricing, and the schema cookbook. We'll provision bench access and schedule a POC kickoff.
10:49 Daniel Park: Sounds good. Couple final clarifications: sandbox keys will have the same constraints as production for the POC?
10:55 Alex Nguyen: They will be rate-limited but can mirror production route configs. For full isolation we can spin up a customer-dedicated sandbox.
11:05 Hannah Kim: We'll send contact for compliance and our SCIM metadata by Monday.
11:09 Alex Nguyen: Excellent. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with an email and links.
11:14 Evan Brooks: Thanks all, that was useful.
11:17 [call ends]
